Distinguishing clinical features Other nutritional deficiencies often present Serum calcium is tightly regulated by parathy roid hormone (PTH) and vitamin D. In the setting of low serum calcium, PTH acts to increase active vitamin D (1,25(OH)2D3) in the kidney which then increases calcium absorption in the small intestine. Bone is the largest calcium reservoir in the body and is released by the indirect action of PTH on osteoclastic bone resorption [3]. The production of biologically active 1,25(OH)2D3 begins in the skin where UV light alters the structure of 7-dehydrocholesterol into vitamin D3. Vitamin D can also be obtained through intake of fatty fish in the diet, or as vitamin D2 from supplements, plants, and fungi. Activation of vitamin D occurs in a stepwise fashion by cytochrome P450 enzymes located in various tissues through the body [4]. In the liver, CYP2R1 is the major 25-hydroxylase enzyme catalyzing conversion of vitamin D to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, though multiple CYP enzymes have some degree of 25-hydroxylase activity [5]. The kidney is the major site of synthesis of active vitamin D (1,25(OH)2D3) via 1α-hydroxylase activity of CYP27B1. 1,25(OH)2D3 binds the vitamin D receptor (VDR), which serves as a transcription factor altering gene expression impacting both cal cium and phosphate homeostasis [6]. Higher 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations increase small intestine absorption of phosphate via the vitamin D dependent sodium-phosphate 2b (NaPi-2b) cotransporter. High 1,25(OH)2D3 and/or calcium reduce PTH secretion thereby indirectly increasing phos phate reabsorption in the kidney. In contrast, 1,25(OH)2D3 increases FGF23 production in osteocytes which subsequently enhances renal phosphate excretion [3]. PTH decreases phosphate reabsorption by reducing NaPi-2a and NaPi-2c cotransporters in the renal proximal tubule thereby increas ing phosphate excretion in the urine. PTH is a potent stimulator of 1α-hydroxylase activity thereby increasing 1,25(OH)2D3 production, which indirectly activates osteoclastic bone reabsorption releasing both calcium and phosphate into the extracellular space [3]. FGF23 is produced in osteocytes under the influence of 1,25(OH)2D3 and phosphate concentrations. Like PTH, FGF23 decreases phosphate reabsorption in the kidney by decreasing NaPi-2a and NaPi-2c cotransports in the proximal tubule. Although several skeletal dys plasias demonstrate overlapping features with rickets, Blount disease, Schmid type metaphy seal chondrodysplasia, and hypophosphatasia (HPP) are three important disorders to con sider when evaluating a child with suspected rickets. Blount disease presents with unilateral or bilateral tibial bowing and varus deformity and is due to asymmetric growth at the tibial growth plate. Radiographic findings show varus angulation of the metaphysis and wid ening and irregularity at the medial growth plate of the tibia with breaking of the medial part of the epiphysis [85]. Laboratory evalua tion is normal, and management is surgical correction of the deformity when severe. Radiographic findings can be difficult to distin guish from rickets and demonstrate growth plate irregularity and flaring [86]. As with Blount disease, laboratory assessment of vita min D and mineral homeostasis are normal. Hypophosphatasia (HPP) is caused by pathogenic variants of the tissue nonspecific alkaline phosphatase gene located on chromo some 1. Clinical severity is broad, ranging from death in the neonatal period to early loss of deciduous teeth with the root fully intact and no detectable skeletal abnormalities [87]. Autosomal recessive inheritance predicts more ## PDF page 547 | printed page 541 severe disease compared to those with a single allele mutation. Radiographs reveal extensive under mineralization of the entire skeleton in the most severely affected. Children with less severe disease have findings localized to the growth plates characterized by radiolucent bands that extend from the physis into the metaphysis of long bones. Although this radiographic appearance helps distinguish HPP from other forms of rickets, the most important difference between HPP and rickets is the presence of low serum alkaline phos phatase activity. Family history can identify many with herita ble disease. A thorough exam should include assessment of growth, limb deformities, and coexisting disorders (as detailed above) that may provide insight into the underlying pathology. History and examination are often sufficient to establish the cause of rickets such as in a child with family history of XLH or a breastfed infant with dark skin pigment with no vitamin D supplementation. Although some genetic forms of rickets can be associated with unique clinical fea tures, the general findings of rickets are con sistent regardless of the underlying mechanism leading to disease. Presenting clinical features will depend on severity and duration of rick ets, as well as the patient’s age and develop mental abilities, which alter the mechanical forces applied to the bone. Infants with rickets may have abnormal head shape due to positional changes and pal pable craniotabes (softening of the skull bones) in the setting of undermineralized and thin bone. A prominent forehead (frontal bossing) and delayed closure of fontanelles may be present. The “rachitic rosary” (enlarge ment of the costochondral joints) may be vis ible or palpable on the anterior chest. Although not unique to children with rickets, a horizonal concavity (Harrison’s groove or sulcus) originating from the attachment of the diaphragm at the sixth costal cartilage that is exaggerated with contraction of the dia phragm during inspiration may be present [88]. As discussed earlier in this chapter, it is criti cal to remember that nutritional rickets is a preventable disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics, Endocrine Society, Institute of Medicine (IOM), and a Global Consensus of experts all endorse 400 IU vitamin D intake daily for infants up to 12 months of age for prevention of rickets. It is uncertain if 400 IU is sufficient for optimal bone health and growth but has been clearly shown to prevent rickets in this age group. IOM and the Global Consensus recommend 600 IU vitamin D for children over 12 months of age. Adequate cal cium intake is also required to prevent rickets. According to the IOM, children up to 6 months of age should receive 200 mg cal cium per day and 260 mg per day for those 6–12 months old. The Global Consensus guideline recommends 500 mg calcium intake per day as sufficient for children after 12 months of age. We and others endorse the IOM recommendation for progressively increasing calcium intake through childhood from 700 mg per day after 12 months of age up to 1300 mg per day starting at age 9 years up to 17 years old, a time when linear growth and thus skeletal mineral demands are high. Multiple dosing regimens for vitamin D have been reported as effective in healing nutrition rickets including daily oral dosing and intermittent high dose therapy (as high as 600,000 IU as a single dose) given orally or intramuscularly. As noted above, vitamin D intake of 400 IU per day for all infants is endorsed by several organizations and has been shown to prevent rickets [10, 13, 91–93]. Although this amount may be sufficient to prevent rickets, it is insufficient for treatment of established disease. Global Consensus guidelines recommend oral treatment with 2000 IU vitamin D per day for at least 3 months for all ages [10]. Oral therapy is rec ommended over intramuscular therapy, and “stoss” therapy, where very large doses are administered on one or over several days, due to the risk of vitamin D toxicity leading to hypercalciuria and/or hypercalcemia [94]. Calcium supplementation is recommended during treatment of vitamin D deficiency rickets, even in those without hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia may occur with vitamin D replacement as mineral is deposited in the skeleton and as PTH levels fall. For those who are eucalcemic or mildly hypocalcemic, oral dosing is sufficient. However, severe symp tomatic hypocalcemia does occur that can cause seizures, tetany, laryngospasm, and car diomyopathy with fatalities being reported. Children with severe, symptomatic hypocalce mia due to nutritional rickets require hospital ization for intravenous calcium administration and monitoring until an oral regimen can be established that maintains serum calcium in a safe range. Various dosing recommendations exist for calcium including weight-based dosing (35–75 mg elemental calcium per kilogram per day in 2–3 divided doses) or a simple fixed dose of 500 mg per day regardless of age or weight [10, 16]. The recommendation for both vitamin D and calcium supplementation for treatment of nutritional rickets acknowledges ## PDF page 552 | printed page 546 the often-coexisting low calcium intake of those with vitamin D deficiency and that some degree of vitamin D deficiency can be over come by adequate calcium intake. Calcium carbonate should be taken with food to allow appropriate absorption, while calcium citrate can be taken on an empty stomach [95]. It is important to clarify with parents how to assess the dose of calcium provided by vari ous calcium preparations. Calcium carbonate is 40% elemental calcium by weight (i.e., 1000 mg calcium carbonate contains only 400 mg of elemental calcium). Likewise, cal cium citrate contains 21% elemental calcium and calcium glubionate 6.5% elemental cal cium by weight. Confirmation of the elemen tal calcium intake is crucial, primarily to prevent underdosing. While uncommon in the US, nutritional rickets due to calcium deficiency without vita min D deficiency is well described in other regions and has been successfully treated with calcium alone [96]. A randomized controlled trial conducted in Nigerian children revealed that in children with calcium deficiency rick ets, treatment with calcium alone or calcium plus vitamin D was more effective than treat ment with vitamin D alone [97]. Response to therapy should be monitored not only for efficacy but also for potential tox icity. Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin and as such, excess administration can result in long standing toxicity. The frequency of monitor ing depends on the severity of disease and the presence and severity of hypocalcemia. Even in severe disease, serum calcium, phosphorus, and PTH can normalize in days to weeks. However, alkaline phosphatase and radio graphic changes often take months to normal ize. For most children (excluding those with severe hypocalcemia), we recommend measur ing serum calcium phosphorus, creatinine, PTH, total alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D 2–3 weeks after initiating therapy and after dose adjustments if required. Less frequent monitoring is required once biochemical parameters are improving. We recommend obtaining radiographs 2–3 months after initi ating therapy to document improvement or resolution of rickets. Treatment doses of vita ### 21 min D and calcium are recommended for at least 3 months, but some may require a longer duration to exhibit full healing of rickets. Urine calcium (24 our collection or calcium to creatinine ratio) is helpful in monitoring for efficacy and toxicity. Initially, urine calcium is low due to inadequate absorption and deposi tion into bone. Urine calcium can remain rela tively low until the rickets resolves and the bone reservoir for mineral has been suffi ciently filled. Once biochemical and radiographic reso lution of rickets has been established, preven tion of recurrence requires maintenance dosing of vitamin D and adequate calcium intake via diet and/or supplementation. Even within the same family, disease manifes tations and need for treatment can vary widely during adulthood requiring an individualized treatment plan. For those treated with buro sumab, dosing is every 2 weeks during child hood and every 4 weeks for adults. Our approach is similar to conventional therapy by transitioning to the adult dosing frequency after cessation of linear growth (preferably closer to the time of peak bone mass). Complicating this transition is the readiness of an adolescent to assume more responsibil ity for their own care as they become young adults and often move away from home for college or work. Guiding principles have been published to assist in this transition for young adults with XLH [117]. ### 21.9.3.2 Other FGF23-Mediated ### Disorders Specific guidelines for the treatment of other FGF23 mediated hypophosphatemic disor ders are not as robust as those for XLH. However, the same principles of con ventional therapy with phosphate and cal citriol therapy as noted above can be used [118]. Titration of doses, laboratory monitor ing, and screening for complications, includ ing secondary hyperparathyroidism and nephrocalcinosis, are the same as manage ment for XLH. ADHR is unique in that the disease course can wax and wane over time, thus not always requiring lifelong treatment [43]. This phe nomenon may be partly related to the interac tion of iron deficiency leading to increased FGF23 production which cannot be efficiently inactivated in patients with ADHR [44]. Kapelari et al. reported a 5-year-old girl with ADHR with clinical features of rickets coex isting with low iron stores but resolution of rickets without need for calcitriol and phos phate therapy after iron deficiency was cor rected [119]. Thus, monitoring and treating iron deficiency may preclude the need for cal citriol and phosphate in some with ADHR. Successful treatment of hypophospha temic rickets caused by the various forms of ARHR, fibrous dysplasia of bone, and CSHS with oral phosphate and calcitriol have been reported [50, 56, 59, 62, 120]. There has been speculation that removal of epidermal nevi causing CSHS might improve hypophosphatemia, but no therapeu tic benefit has been found in patients with excision or ablation of nevi [62, 121]. Successful treatment with off label use of medications targeting the underlying disease mechanism have been reported. One patient had improvement in clinical, biochemical, and radiographic signs of rickets with a mito gen-activated protein kinase (MEK) inhibitor, which acts directly on the RAS/MAPK path way [122]. Use of burosumab has been explored (off label) for FGF23 mediated conditions other than XLH and TIO. Normalization of serum phosphate and improved clinical outcomes related to rickets in multiple patients with CSHS treated with burosumab has been described [123, 124]. Likewise, use in a 7-yearold boy with severe fibrous dysplasia led to the normalization of serum phosphate, improve ment in alkaline phosphatase, and resolution of radiographic rachitic changes after 17 months of therapy [125]. Successful use of burosumab for autosomal recessive hypo phosphatemic rickets due to DMP1 muta tions has also been reported [126]. ## PDF page 558 | printed page 552 TIO is unique among the FGF23 medi ated disorders in that it can be cured assuming the offending tumor can be localized and removed. It is, therefore, important to con sider this diagnosis in a child with acquired disease in whom an alternate cause of FGF23 mediated rickets is not identified. After com plete resection, FGF23, phosphate, and 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations normalize over days to weeks. Normalization of alkaline phosphatase and radiographic change of rick ets/osteomalacia can take months. For those with disease that cannot be localized or resected medical therapy (calcitriol and phos phate or burosumab) should be initiated [65, 66]. Burosumab has been approved for treat ment of TIO when surgical cure is not possi ble [127]. ### 21.9.3.3 Non-FGF23 Mediated ### Hypophosphatemia Similar to FGF23 mediated hypophospha temic disorders, hereditary hypophospha temic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH) caused by SLC34A3 mutations leads to renal phosphate wasting. However, in contrast to FGF23 mediated disease, 1α-hydroxylase activity is high since FGF23 concentrations are appropriately low. As a result, 1,25(OH)2D3 concentrations can be markedly elevated lead ing to increased intestinal calcium absorption and hypercalciuria. This distinction is impor tant in that treatment consists of phosphate supplementation alone without calcitriol since endogenous 1,25(OH)2D3 production is already high. Additional calcitriol would exacerbate the hypercalciuria and nephrocal cinosis. Phosphate administration also serves to limit intestinal calcium absorption and can reduce endogenous 1,25(OH)2D3 production, both of which lessen the degree of hypercalci uria. With phosphate supplementation, bone pain and muscle strength improve, radio graphic evidence of rickets (if present) can resolve, urine calcium excretion is reduced, and serum alkaline phosphatase levels improve [71, 72]. Renal Fanconi syndrome is a complex col lection of disorders. Hypophosphatemia can be treated with phosphate supplementation. ### 21 Bicarbonate replacement therapy may also improve the associated bone disease. When possible, treatment of the underlying disorder causing proximal tubular dysfunction may preclude the need for phosphate replacement therapy. Likewise, for children with nutri tional phosphate deficiency, correction of the underlying malabsorptive disease or the addi tion of phosphate to the diet (or via a supple ment) will resolve the hypophosphatemia and associated rickets. ### 21.10 Summary Rickets constitutes a broad spectrum of dis eases leading to a common clinical disorder of impaired growth plate and skeletal mineral ization. Although entirely preventable and despite campaigns to raise awareness, nutri tional rickets due to vitamin D and/or calcium deficiency remains a frequent cause of mor bidity worldwide. Treatment of nutritional rickets is fairly straightforward but continued public health efforts aimed at prevention remain of utmost importance. Our under standing of the molecular cause of many heri table forms of rickets has expanded in recent years with targeted therapy now available for some. History, exam, and relatively few labo ratory tests can identify the underlying cause of rickets for most which allows use of disease specific treatment strategies in an effort to optimize long-term outcomes. ### References 1.
